text:
Here is a parent-facing explanation you could use or adapt:

---

## Why we are moving to mixed-attainment maths teaching

We are changing the way maths is taught so that children of different starting points learn together in the same class.

We know this change may worry some parents. Some people feel that children learn best when they are grouped by ability. We understand that view. We are making this change because we believe it will help more children make strong progress in maths, while also keeping their confidence and enjoyment of the subject.

## What mixed-attainment means

In mixed-attainment classes, children with a range of starting points work together in the same lesson.

This does **not** mean every child is doing exactly the same task all the time.

Teachers still make sure work is suitable for each child. They do this by:
- asking different questions,
- giving different levels of support,
- using activities that can be tackled in different ways,
- helping children move on when they are ready.

## Why we are changing

### 1. Children are not fixed as “low”, “middle” or “high” ability
A child who finds one topic hard may do very well in another. Children can grow quickly when they are taught well, given time, and supported carefully.

Grouping children by ability can sometimes make it harder for them to move on. Mixed-attainment teaching keeps the door open for every child to make progress.

### 2. Children benefit from learning together
Children learn in different ways from each other. In a mixed class:
- children hear different ways of thinking,
- children can explain ideas to each other,
- children learn that there is often more than one way to solve a problem,
- children develop confidence by talking about maths.

### 3. It helps avoid labelling
When children are placed in “top”, “middle” or “bottom” sets, they can begin to see themselves as that label. Some children lose confidence and stop believing they can improve.

We want every child to feel that maths is something they can get better at.

### 4. It can lead to better teaching
In mixed-attainment classes, teachers plan carefully for a range of needs. This often leads to lessons with:
- clearer explanations,
- more discussion,
- more checking for understanding,
- more opportunities for all children to think deeply.

## What this means for your child

Your child will still be taught in a way that meets their needs.

They may:
- work on the same topic as the rest of the class,
- have support if they need it,
- be challenged if they are ready for more,
- be asked to explain their thinking,
- practise until they are secure.

We want every child to keep moving forward. No child will be held back, and no child will be left behind.

## What this does not mean

This change does **not** mean:
- that children will be left to struggle on their own,
- that the work will be too hard,
- that stronger mathematicians will not be challenged,
- that teachers will not know each child’s needs.

Good mixed-attainment teaching is carefully planned and well supported.

## Why we believe this is the right choice

Our aim is for every child to become a confident mathematician. We want children to:
- understand maths deeply,
- be able to explain their thinking,
- enjoy tackling problems,
- believe they can improve.

We believe mixed-attainment teaching gives more children the chance to do this.

## We will keep you informed

We know this is an important change. We will continue to share information with you about:
- how maths is taught,
- how your child is doing,
- how you can help at home.

If you have questions or concerns, please speak to us. We value your views and we want to work in partnership with you.

---
